clinicalPearls: ATTR arises from transthyretin, a hepatically synthesised transport protein for thyroxine and retinol-binding protein; disease reflects dissociation of its stabilising tetramer into amyloidogenic monomers.
Two forms exist: hereditary variant disease (ATTRv) from autosomal dominant TTR mutations, and acquired wild-type disease (ATTRwt), which predominantly affects older men with a cardiac phenotype.
Genotype shapes phenotype: Val30Met tends toward polyneuropathy with endemic clusters in Portugal, Sweden and Japan, whereas Val122Ile and Thr60Ala favour cardiomyopathy.
Cardiac ATTR presents as heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, increased ventricular wall thickness on echocardiography, and a discordantly low-voltage or pseudo-infarct ECG.
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis and spontaneous biceps tendon rupture are red-flag musculoskeletal harbingers that often precede cardiac disease by years.
Bone-avid scintigraphy with technetium-labelled DPD, PYP or HMDP showing grade 2 to 3 myocardial uptake, once a monoclonal protein is excluded, permits a non-biopsy diagnosis of cardiac ATTR.

Disease-modifying options include transthyretin tetramer stabilisers and gene-silencing agents (small interfering RNA and antisense oligonucleotides); liver transplantation historically removed the variant protein source.
Autonomic neuropathy with orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal dysmotility and erectile dysfunction is prominent in the neuropathic form and limits tolerance of heart failure therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Transthyretin circulates as a homotetramer; destabilisation, driven either by an inherited point mutation in ATTRv or by ageing-related factors acting on the normal sequence in ATTRwt, promotes dissociation into monomers that misfold and aggregate into insoluble amyloid fibrils. These fibrils deposit in the extracellular matrix of the myocardium, peripheral and autonomic nerves, and the tenosynovium and ligaments, producing a stiff non-compliant myocardium and length-dependent axonal degeneration. The relative tropism for heart versus nerve is strongly influenced by the specific mutation, whereas wild-type disease is almost exclusively cardiac and musculoskeletal. Deposition is progressive and, untreated, culminates in restrictive cardiomyopathy with conduction disease or disabling sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Hypertensive heart disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Other infiltrative cardiomyopathies (Fabry disease, cardiac sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis)
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy and diabetic polyneuropathy
Hereditary sensorimotor neuropathies such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography with longitudinal strain showing apical sparing
Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and T1 or extracellular volume mapping
Bone scintigraphy with DPD, PYP or HMDP graded by the Perugini scale
Serum free light chains with serum and urine immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis
TTR gene sequencing to distinguish variant from wild-type disease
Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry when required
Cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP and troponin) and nerve conduction studies according to phenotype
redFlags: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, increased wall thickness and low ECG voltages
Hypotension or intolerance when standard heart failure or antihypertensive drugs are introduced
New high-grade atrioventricular block or need for pacing
Rapidly progressive sensorimotor neuropathy with autonomic failure
reference.prognosis: Untreated cardiac ATTR carries a poor prognosis with median survival of only a few years, although wild-type disease generally progresses more slowly than many variant forms. Stabiliser and gene-silencing therapies now improve survival and functional outcomes, particularly when started early.
pitfalls: Attributing increased ventricular wall thickness to hypertension and missing the diagnosis
Assuming all cardiac amyloid is AL type and delaying bone scintigraphy
Interpreting a positive bone scan as diagnostic without excluding a monoclonal protein, as co-existent MGUS is common in the elderly
Overlooking the early musculoskeletal clues of carpal tunnel syndrome and spinal stenosis
